   Latest stop for tourists on South Korea’s shopping trail? The pharmacy
 Sign up now: Get insights on Asia's fast-moving developments
 Foreign shoppers are increasingly turning to pharmacies with a stronger focus on clinical skincare and functional beauty.
 PHOTO: THE KOREA HERALD/ASIA NEWS NETWORK
 Published   Oct 26, 2026, 11:43 AM
 Updated   Oct 26, 2026, 12:22 PM
 Set as preferred source Listen Summarise Foreign tourists in South Korea are increasingly shopping at pharmacies for authentic red ginseng, skincare and other health products, especially in Seoul’s Myeong-dong.
 Social media and translation apps help visitors find Korean pharmacy items, while many prefer in-person buying for advice and confidence in product authenticity.
 Pharmacies are adapting with multilingual guides, tax refund services and product displays. Foreign card spending hit 2.12 trillion won in May, showing fast growth.
 AI generated
 SEOUL – On a chilly October afternoon in Myeong-dong, Seoul’s bustling tourist shopping district, Vietnamese tourist Nguyen Lan was browsing the shelves of a pharmacy for red ginseng, a favourite dietary supplement for many South Koreans.
 She used Google Translate to ask the pharmacist how much it cost, what its benefits were and when to take it.
 Although Korean red ginseng is readily available in Vietnam, Lan said she preferred buying it in a pharmacy here in person because she felt more confident about its authenticity.
 “Finding authentic products (in Vietnam) can be difficult because of counterfeit products and mislabelled imports,” Lan told The Korea Herald.
 “Shopping at pharmacies also seems like a chance to find products that meet our needs and bring home a piece of everyday Korean life, since we don’t get to travel to Korea that often,” Lan noted.
 At a nearby pharmacy, groups of Japanese and Chinese tourists scanned the store for skincare products, treatments and ointments to take home.
 A Japanese tourist in her 40s, who wished to remain anonymous, said she was looking for ointments to fade dark spots and blemishes on her cheeks.
 She showed the pharmacist a shopping list on her phone, written in Korean and ranging from acne treatments and scar ointments to vitamins, cold remedies and pain relief patches. After the pharmacist suggested some similar products, she used a translation app to read the labels and compare them.
 While Japan is known for its wide selection of over-the-counter medicines, health products and beauty items at pharmacies and discount chains like Don Quijote, she said South Korean pharmacies had carved out their own niche by offering specialised skincare products that are harder to find in Japan.
 “Pharmacies in South Korea offer specialised clinical-grade skincare and high-strength treatments. They are more varied in South Korea than in Japan, and some brands are developed by dermatologists and are less expensive than luxury brands,” she said.
 “Also, I prefer shopping for pharmacy products in person so I can take a closer look and ask a pharmacist for advice.”
 New destination for foreign shoppers
 The shoppers’ experiences show how South Korea’s beauty appeal extends beyond cosmetics stores to pharmacy shelves.
 Beyond beauty retailers such as Olive Young, Chicor and Daiso, foreign shoppers are increasingly turning to pharmacies with a stronger focus on clinical skincare and functional beauty, boasting products tailored to concerns such as acne, dark spots and sensitive skin.
 Products popular on social media, including Madeca Cream, Easydew and Rejuvenex PDRN ( polydeoxyribonucleotide ) creams, are often more readily available at pharmacies than at mainstream beauty retailers.
 Posts and videos featuring “must-buy” South Korean pharmacy products on social media platforms TikTok , X, Xiaohongshu and Instagram suggest that visitors arrive knowing which brands to look for. Some users have also created English-language maps of Seoul pharmacies, listing their locations, opening hours and product ranges.
 Foreign visitors spent 2.12 trillion won (S$2.06 billion) by card in South Korea in May, surpassing 2 trillion won for the first time, according to data on foreign tourists’ card spending released by the Korea Tourism Organization (KTO) in June.
 The data showed that pharmacy spending jumped 15,249% in Seongsu 2-ga 1-dong and 2,877% in Seongsu 2-ga 3-dong, both in Seoul. Spending also surged 12,828% in U 1-dong in Busan’s Haeundae-gu, a rise KTO cited as evidence that the trend was spreading beyond the capital.

 KTO attributed part of the growth to visitors buying skin-repair creams and other products at pharmacies after cosmetic procedures at dermatology clinics, as quality healthcare, affordable treatments and the popularity of K-beauty draw visitors to South Korea for medical care and wellness experiences.
 To meet growing demand, Cresoty, a Seoul-based leading healthcare IT solutions company, launched K-Pharm on Oct 14 in partnership with KTO, helping foreign tourists find pharmacies and access discount coupons and tax refund services.
 Targeting global shoppers
 Pharmacies are adapting to foreign demand by displaying popular products near the entrance and offering guides in English, Chinese and Japanese.
 Some also have staff dedicated to helping foreign shoppers or separate checkout counters, reflecting a wider shift in tourist shopping, with independent travellers venturing beyond department stores and duty-free shops.
 Some pharmacies even resemble beauty boutiques, with neatly arranged displays, multilingual assistance and tax refund services for foreign shoppers.
 Beyond language assistance, many South Korean pharmacies are expanding their beauty and wellness offerings to include products formulated for specific concerns, including acne, redness, dark spots and skin recovery, which are also widely popular among tourists from overseas.
 Recently, PDRN, an ingredient used in products marketed for skin repair, has become a particular draw, according to pharmacist Oh Ji-eun, who runs a pharmacy in Seoul’s Myeong-dong.
 She noted that its popularity grew especially after South Korean aesthetic clinics began using it in treatments aimed at improving skin recovery and hydration.
 Oh also noted differences in shopping preferences among tourists from different countries.
 Japanese visitors often look for hydroquinone creams – topical skin-lightening and bleaching agents used to treat hyperpigmentation – for dark spots, glutathione products marketed for skin brightening and anti-perspirants. Shoppers from English-speaking and other Western countries tend to be more interested in anti-ageing skincare than medicines, the pharmacist said.
 Oh added that acne treatments, pharmacy-exclusive skincare products and pimple patches are popular among foreign shoppers of all nationalities. Chinese-speaking customers also buy a broader range of medicines, including pain relief patches.
 “Foreign tourists often come in looking for skincare products they have seen on social media and end up buying cold medicines, vitamins and pain relief patches as well. It seems like many are willing to try products simply because they are South Korean ,” Oh said. THE KOREA HERALD/ASIA NEWS NETWORK
